title: Sarmale
subtitle: Romanian stuffed cabbage rolls in tomato sauce
excerpt: Cabbage leaves are stuffed with a mix of beef and pork mince with raw rice, then slow-simmered in a tomato sauce for two hours until tender throughout. Sarmale are Romania's most beloved dish, eaten at Christmas and Easter. The recipe comes from Ottoman influence -- dolma that became entirely Romanian.
sourceNotes: Sarmale are Romania's most beloved dish. They are eaten at Christmas, Easter, and every major celebration. The recipe comes from Ottoman influence -- dolma spread across the Balkans and became local everywhere it landed. In Romania, pork and rice rolls in cabbage leaves are the definitive version.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze cooked rolls in sauce for up to 3 months.

content.text: The key to sarmale is using raw rice in the filling. It absorbs the juices during cooking and binds the filling from inside. Pre-cooked rice will make the rolls dense and the filling dry. The rolling takes practice but even imperfect rolls taste right.

Bring a large pot of water to the boil. Submerge the whole cabbage and cook for 5-10 minutes until the outer leaves loosen. Peel off leaves carefully, returning to hot water as needed. Cool and pat dry.
Cut out the thick central rib from each leaf.
Mix beef mince, pork mince, raw rice, grated onion, salt, and pepper together well.
Place 2 generous tablespoons of filling on each leaf near the base. Fold in the sides, then roll up tightly.
Line the base of a large heavy pot with bacon rashers. Arrange rolls seam-side down in tight layers. Mix tinned tomatoes with tomato puree and pour over. Tuck in thyme sprigs.
Add enough water to just cover. Cover tightly and simmer on a very low heat for 2 hours. Check occasionally and add a splash of water if needed.

items.symptom: Rolls are dense and the rice is chewy
items.cause: Rice was pre-cooked or rolls packed too tightly
items.fix: Use raw rice -- it absorbs the cooking juices and expands naturally. Don't pack rolls tightly in the pot.

content.text: Romania, but also across the Balkans -- Serbia, Croatia, Bulgaria. Every culture claims them. In Romania they are inseparable from Christmas and are made in large batches to last over the holiday.
